newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Mediator meets calm in Central African Republic.
newsitem.headline: Mediator meets calm in Central African Republic.

text.p: Respected Malian mediator Amadou Toumnani Toure arrived in the Central African Republic capital Bangui on a calm Wednesday after clashes between African peacekeepers and army mutineers killed at least 80 people.

The fifth day since fighting erupted was quiet, after peacekeepers on Tuesday shelled districts loyal to mutineers, some of whom had not responded to a January 25 deal brokered by Toure to return to their units.

"It's the fourth time I'm coming here to the Central Afdrican Republic. I hope it's the last time that I come to sort out this problem of mutiny," Mali's former military leader told reporters on arrival at Bangui airport.

Over 300 marchers supporting the dissafected soldiers, some carrying bodies, marched to the French embassy to accuse the former colonial power and the peacekeepers of siding with President Ange-Felix Patasse.

The local Red Cross said it had been swamped by the arrival of tens of thousands of people who fled the southern districts loyal to mutineers, which the peacekeepers bombarded with shells from tanks and heavy mortars.

"There is not enough drinking water, there is not enough food," Dr David Dofara, head of the local Red Cross, told Reuters. He said the number of people displaced by fighting rose to over 40,000 on Wednesday from around 8,000 before.
The death toll on Wednesday rose to at least 80, with an estimated 150 people injured, Dofara said.

A spokesman for the African force, sent to bring peace after a string of mutinies between pro- and anti-Patasse army factions, said the force had handed 85 mutineers captured in fighting to the Presidential Guard.

The January peace deal the African force came to implement was preceded by three mutinies in less than a year in which political and ethnic supporters of Patasse in the army clashed with former comrades.

French troops are stationed in Bangui under a defence accord, but the former colonial power, which last year intervened to stop clashes, denied on Tuesday they were directly helping the African force.
Paris on Wednesday urged mutineers and private militia to give up their arms, warning that failure to do so could plunge the nation into new fighting.
The French foreign ministry said 28 French nationals including numerous children had been flown out of Bangui on Tuesday in a military aircraft.

After the latest battles, Bangui's African force is looking less like a model for bringing peace to Brazzaville, capital of the neighbouring Congo -- where it has been touted as a possible solution after over two weeks of clashes.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 in Bangui began as protests over pay but evolved into a movement to topple Patasse, a civilian from the north, elected in 1993. The third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Most of the mutineers are members of the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.

The 800-strong African force includes soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo. A Senegalese soldier killed on Friday was among the first casualties. A Chadian soldier was also among the dead.
